segments.title: How the Royal Navy shaped the Skua specification
segments.summary: The Skua was ordered in 1934 under a new operational requirement process that let the Royal Navy state what it needed and left the Air Ministry to write the specification.
segments.body: The Skua's 1934 order came from a new way of defining British naval aircraft. The Royal Navy stated the capability it wanted, and the Air Ministry converted that request into a formal specification. Earlier institutional debate had failed to give the service an aircraft built to dive-bomb, let alone a dedicated dive bomber. Direct naval control over requirements made the Skua's design possible.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the Royal Navy's direct input into aircraft specifications and its earlier lack of a purpose-built dive bomber.

segments.title: Henderson's fighter-dive-bomber specification
segments.summary: Rear Admiral Henderson used his carrier experience as Third Sea Lord to shape the requirement for an aircraft that could serve as both fighter and dive bomber.
segments.body: Rear Admiral Henderson, the Third Sea Lord, became closely involved in writing the new specification. His previous responsibility for aircraft carriers gave him direct experience of carrier aviation. The brief called for a fighter-dive-bomber, so the Skua had to serve two operational roles. This is the design problem to keep in mind when the video turns to its engine, guns, speed, and range.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies Rear Admiral Henderson's involvement and the resulting fighter-dive-bomber specification.

segments.title: Why the Skua needed more power, armament, speed, and range
segments.summary: An 890-horsepower Bristol Perseus XII and four forward-firing .303-inch Browning machine guns limited the Skua. Greater speed and range might have made it far more capable.
segments.body: The Skua's shortcomings appear here as a linked set of design limits. Its 890-horsepower Bristol Perseus XII supplied the power, while four forward-firing .303-inch Browning machine guns made up the fixed gun armament. More power and heavier firepower, together with slightly greater speed and range, could have produced a very capable aircraft. The passage weighs the whole performance package instead of blaming one component.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies the engine and guns, then says greater speed and range would have improved the aircraft.

segments.title: Königsberg and the Skua's short technological lead
segments.summary: The Skua sank Königsberg and achieved more than its reputation suggests, yet rapid change in aircraft design soon overtook a type that had begun at the leading edge.
segments.body: The sinking of Königsberg shows why the Skua cannot be dismissed as an operational failure. It entered service during an unusually fast transition in aircraft design. A machine conceived at the leading edge could be overtaken soon after it appeared. The Skua was still a good aircraft in this account, even though later developments exposed its limits.

evidence.note: The transcript cites the sinking of Königsberg and describes the Skua as a rapidly surpassed but still good aircraft.
